3610 Metropolitan, and today is July the 20th.

M-E-L-E-Y. M-E-L-E-Y. And, uh, what's your name? Herb Freewell. A little louder, please. Herb Freewell. Okay. Pick it up? Yeah, I think it's picking you up. And, uh, my name is Dick Allen. Let me move this, uh, machine a little here. I'll turn it off for a second. Okay, I think we've, uh, we got it going now, alright? First thing I'm gonna ask you is exactly where were you born? You know?
Yeah, I was born on here, cause of my knowledge, on here on, uh, on, uh, Cluett and Claiborne. Cluett and Claiborne. That's when I was like, yeah. Mm-hmm.
And, uh, what was your, uh, exact date of birth now again?
Boy? Mm-hmm. Well, I was, uh, born in 1892. Mm-hmm. That's on the 18th day of February. 18th day of February.

That's right. Alright.
Let me see now. I wanted to ask you about your uncle the first thing, and, well, the first thing I wanna ask you really is, uh, about, uh, who in your family played music before you?
Before I played? Well, I had my, one of my uncle of mine played music. He was a Kramers player.
Mm-hmm.
His name was Taton Bonds.
Taton, mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.

He was Kramers.
No, I mean, what style, what kind? Did he play, uh, what you'd call progressive, or?
No, I wanted to, uh, on our common music, same as we play here. Not much in the music.
Mostly, uh, he didn't read then, huh?
No, not much of a read on us. Mm-hmm. Most pick up. The majority was this.
Well, when did he die, do you know?
Well, he kind of got me on that. It's been quite a while, and I was a part of a kid then.
You were a kid when he died, huh? Yeah, I was a kid then. Were you in short pants when he died?
I think I was in dresses, for a mistake.
Do you remember him then, yourself?
Well, I don't know. Well, I don't know. Could I have remembered him?
Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.
You remember his music clearly.
Yeah, partly clearly I don't remember his music. He used to be with a bass and ghetto, mandolin, violin, crowning. That was the most of the music then time. How do you call that? The carding.
Mm-hmm. Did they have any trumpets now?
No, they never used trumpets much. I don't remember using any trumpets at all.
Did he play steady jobs, or would he be a serenade on one?
No, no, there's different parties, what you call surprise parties and boy state parties, you know, entertaining different ways.
Have trombones in the band then?
Well, I remember trombones being in the band then. I just remember his right name, but we always called him Long Charlie. Long Charlie. Yeah, he was a vowel trombone player.
Well, how did they play that vowel trombone?
That vowel trombone was in the same honor as the trumpet.
Mm-hmm.
That three keys, the same as the trumpet had, the finger.
Well, what kind of a part would they play? Would they play this?
That was a trombone part.
Yeah? Well, they couldn't make those slides, couldn't they?
There was no sliding, no, that was more like a bass clip.
Yeah, and they would play a trombone part, but they wouldn't go . No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. Could you sing a little of what they did?

No, you got me now on that. You're not a singer. You're not a singer. In fact, I couldn't sing the blues. So, it was just like, for instance, you see a trumpet. Mm-hmm. Remember all the trumpets they had was about that long?
Yeah.
The trumpet actually was about that long. Mm-hmm. Well, this was a trombone. It's the same thing the trombone you got now. Mm-hmm. But it had a valve to it.
Oh, I've seen them, but I mean, what I want to get at is, did they play lead, or did they play bum, bum, bum, bum, bum, bum, bum, bum, bum.
No, no, this is a band.
Like a bass.
A band. A band. A band. Yeah, this is a band.
Oh, I see.
That's just the same identical thing as the bass, you can see. Yeah, it was the same thing, one was more up and the other was more down. That's all.
Well, what about, uh, how did guys like Willie Cornish and Frankie Deucon play valve? Did you ever hear them play valve?
Well, yeah. It's gonna go on.
Hold on a second.
Go through. Just a minute.
All right, we'll hold it a minute more. Okay. We got it going, man.
I'll put that fan in here. No, no, this is fine.

I'm plenty cool. Uh, now I was wondering about this guy, uh, Tato, you know, I'm not going to play, and, uh, I'd say, would you say that he played anything like Willie Cornish and Frankie Deucon? Yeah.
When they played valve? That's right. Of the same order. Jupiter, T, and that bunch, that's all was valve players too. Ambrose. Those men played valve.
What is Ambrose's right name?
Do you know?
Powers. His name was Ambrose Powers? Powers, yeah. I figured you'd know that. He's supposed to be related to Toka somewhere.

That's right. That's the uncle of Toka. That's Ambrose Powers. He played, uh, well, he, uh, he played, uh, guitar, violin, and trombone. Oh, sure. I didn't know that. Yeah, he played things pretty good. He played mandolin too. Did you ever work with him much? Oh, that's my first start with them men. Yeah, he's one of the men that carried me out. Yeah, he's one of the men that first carried me out between, uh, you can say, uh, him and, uh, T. Rochon, Gilles Duvarny. Well, those men, uh, carried me out.
And what did they play?
Well, that was guitar. And, uh, Rochon T played, uh, bass. And Gilles, he played bass, uh, guitar. Gilles Duvarny did.
He played guitar? Yeah. And, uh, when you first went out with Ambrose, what did he play at that time?
Well, I first went out with Ambrose then, he was playing, uh, violin. Uh-huh. Yeah, he was playing violin during that time.
And who did he have in his band?

Well, let's see, now you know what I mean? Well, it's been such a time ago, it's pretty tough to get that together. Well, uh, let's see who we got that. We had Ambrose, we had a fella called, uh, Johnny Pridons. And, uh, let's see, Ambrose, Johnny Pridons, that was a bass player too. Uh-huh. And sometimes T. Rochon, and sometimes, uh, uh, his boy Gilles Duvarny, ghetto. Uh-huh. Then we had this other one who used to play ghetto with us at times, uh, uh, T-Bar Francis. Is he any relation to Albert Francis?
No, I don't think it's any relation to Albert Francis.
No, I don't think it's any relation to Albert at all, I don't think. Not, not Conor Mano anymore. Uh-huh. No, I don't think.
Did Gilles Duvarny have his own band too?

Well, we all put, partly was in the, hooked up with the same band, cause, uh, you see, in them things we had, let's see, you had the Golden Rule, had the Golden Rule, had the Imperial, you had the Superior, you had the Boys in Blue.
Who were the Boys in Blue?

Well, the Boys in Blue, that was Buddy Petit. That's Buddy Petit, well, sometime you'll get Buddy Petit on that, and you had, uh, the Imperial Band, that was, uh, Johnny Smith. That's Sugar Johnny? Sugar Johnny, you understand? And, uh, well, I don't know, it's a good man of Marquette never get together, I believe it'll take me 50 years to get that together. Yeah. Who was in the Golden Rule?
I can't ever keep that band straight.

That Golden Rule, let's see how the Golden Rule, that Golden Rule, Rondine, they were Gilles Duvarny, and, uh, and, uh, those men would swap up, like, you understand, one man quit here to take another man in his place, you know? Like, Gilles, that was a guitar, and T-Bar was a guitar, we, oh, we had some of them that I really hadn't forgot all about, guitars, basses, and... Well, who managed it at Golden Rule? Well, the Golden Rule was managed one time by Ambrose, and, uh, another time it was managed by Gilles Duvarny, you understand, and the band would jump, you know, like, if you got to work and this band didn't have to work, well, you were looking for work, so you'd go to get to work. And who was the leader? The leader of violin always did lead, it was another violin, the violin didn't lead to the clown, they don't have to lead. And those times? And that's the way that we call it, if it wasn't a violin, you had to go to a clown, see, and that's, the way we got it, now it goes to the trumpet. Them times, it's a different, when you come down to an orchestra or string band, like you say a string band, we would call it, that went to a violin or a clarinet.
What tunes would they play back in those times?

Oh, man, I'll be frank with you, I had to go back some to get them together. But, uh, it was a great deal of Scott Junkins' music. Yeah, they played lots of that stuff, man. I don't think I'd know it for him. While I holler and, uh, blaming on the blues and physical defeat. Oh, man, that's a gang of stuff. Oh, good minutes. Stuff that I just don't know the name of. But that was the most of the music, though, they never played no, uh, make-up numbers, you know? Mm-hmm. That was all solid stuff. High Society, Maryland, and some of that stuff we used to play there, and I don't think I could do anything with it, just direct. Yeah. Do you remember Walla Holla?
Yeah, see, I don't know.
I don't believe I'm in Hummerwood or anything. I don't know Walla Holla. Go with me. I haven't forgotten that thing again. Sounds like down home right down. Mm-hmm. Wow, I can't think of that.
All that stuff has got away from me, man.
I'm playing with these different men that's come along, you know? They pick up, and you come down and something works while it's different.
Well, in that time, you see, that was hard and usually. You see, you get a band, you take a link to a day like on a Sunday, or you catch every

band in town. You see, to have work, you have to have a band, you have to have a band, and you have to have a band. But on the Sundays, you catch them big clubs, they get on out there and they watch for the bands. They get to have their band. They get to have their band. They get to have their band. They get out there and they watch, stand up and watch what band's coming along. The band gets the hot with you on one number, it's carrying your numbers. Well what you do, you go back and what you call the Red Bull, pick one of them old hard numbers off, you throw him off, you see. When you throw him off he'll get neat, you'll get behind him and you wham up. That's where we used to figure it out. But now it's so much different in the music now, I don't know man. There ain't much in the music now. Nobody's playing, it's hard to get a bunch of men together to play music. They ain't going to play the right stuff, they're going to upset all the stuff you've got, they can play it their way. You understand? I understand many bands playing, they tell you it's their number and all that, and you come to find out the peak number come here, some off of this number, some off of that number, some off the other number. Well the majority of them that knew it is gone, so what they're going to do to get them by with? Really if you was to take a bunch of men, pick up a bunch of old time men and get back on their music men like, like you say for instance like Charl and them men that got that stuff and Pete and that, man you'll get back on that stuff man, you'll demand a job. What I mean by demand a job, you want to study how to play it, you wouldn't want to be mixed up here with what you hear now. Because what you hear now ain't but, you can see it's three tunes. Take all that playing right now, ain't but three numbers. You can always put a different tone to it, a different temper to it, or something, you know, put to it to make a sound, but it's the same thing over and over and over. For instance you take one of them and put it right there and start to play it and now you'll get tired of it. You'll get the next one the same thing. Take all these bands here, these old men here, they got some pretty good music they can play there. That music here there's nobody using. You might hear from those big crack shots, you know what I'm saying, you hear them play. You ain't going to hear these, for instance, like you see the bands playing up with one or two hundred men in the band, they're playing that stuff out here with your head and we used to play that stuff with four and five men. You take a climb, they'll land some man, a trumpet, he'll land some maybe a trombone, and he's all around there and he's filling all them little gaps that's left open. Now just direct climb it. Now I tell you now, climb it. Go climb it, nowhere else. Go get there, go bass. Go that one way before man, if you miss you on, man, somebody ride in there on you until you're able to come back. That's different in the music. You never went back and disfigured that, right? I see when we did have the Young Imperial Band, we was out in Charleston, Louisiana, we met, we met, uh, uh, Clayborne Williams out there and we were waiting for a fellow Mr. Roberts and Mr. Settlers. And he told us about, uh, Sharpen Up, because Clayborne Williams had a pretty tough band and he was well liking out there. Well we had a pretty good band. I said, I'm not criticizing your band and nothing, they say, but he's well liking. You know when people like you, they're always going to give you right when you're wrong. Well we didn't sharpen up for him, man. We did. We went back and all that old stuff with Scots music and sharpen up. And the first thing we met him was with high society and high society, dressing, juice, frizzy, the feet and all that stuff would come up there. But when the big thing come off, we had it. He come out with a whole lot of heavy marches and things and heavier bands, but that didn't get it because we was cutting in there with dance music, you see, and, well you see, a few types of dance music and march music. Well he come in with march music. He had one point, we took the three points and gave it to us. We sharpened up on everything they had then, we had a good band. Two of the bands. Barbarin, John Marrero, and, uh, Artemis Don's bass. Let's see, and, Barley called George, we called him Kalkai George. That's the only thing I know about George. He was, uh, he was King the Turca. We had Ambrose, Powers, Wooden Joe. We had Wooden Joe, well, uh, and Ambrose, yeah, Wooden Joe Ambrose. And who else was there? T-Bar, uh, Barbarin. That's the band we had. Well, it was Wooden Joe playing then.
What else? He was playing clarinet. Clarinet. True clarinet.
That's what we had, True clarinet. And I was on clarinet. That sounds good, son, if you can get the right man. True clarinet? You got the right man.
Well, I need to take two clarinet. You take about two or three clarinet, and you can take about two or three clarinet, and you

ain't gonna beat the music. You ain't gonna beat it. off. You ain't gonna beat it. You ain't gonna play no swing music, but you just ride on in there just like a finish off. It wasn't no key to it on the time that we playing. We played music out there with three pieces. Take a bass to get their own clarinet. trying to get on bass and go there, there wasn't no drum, there wasn't no trambones, there wasn't no cornets or nothing like that. Guitar right. But most of that music was no sweet music, it was more like waltzes. See, waltzes, one step, two step, Missouri, Charlotte, slow waltz, fast waltz.
Is that the kind of music your uncle played?

Where? Your uncle. Oh yeah, yeah. He had to talk. That's right, he played for all the, that's soft music too, because in them times they'd play like a surprise party, you understand? Like you had a birthday coming up, well they'd come up and talk with you and wish you a birthday and all that, tell them you go to bed, maybe the wife or friends, somebody who you're with, have it made up. You get a bunch of them, come on here man, knock on the door, excitement, and the band starts playing and they're rushing on you when you open the door man, it's a big excitement. You come together, you've got everything, all the refreshments all together right there. And you're excited, you don't know what to watch.
Did they ever play blues with that kind of a little band? Oh yeah.

In them days, in that time, during that time when the big band started, the bigger band, blues had more of an introduction to it. You see? Had an introduction, but the way it is not all of any tunes is not introduction. Not an ordinary band.
Did you get your clarinet and show us what you mean by an introduction? Well, an introduction is like...

I'll just hum it, either one. Yeah, an introduction is like the old blues, the first blues you have, you're going to play the blues. Three or four times and then it's coming. See? Well that's going on with the old blues. I sing it, I sing it, I sing it. Anything you play, I'll introduce you to the triple beat and the duck, you know, coming on. And it picks up on probably most everything on the chorus. You make a long tune, you have to go over to the chorus and go on over it and come back and go over it again. You get it in the right three or four minutes.
Well when you played tunes that had more than one part to them, what volume would you use, say, at the beginning? How loud would you be?

Well that music like that would run somewhere around about, you see, like soft. See you're loud, then you come soft, then you pick up again, you know. That's the way for it. Anything you play, sometimes it gets so soft on it, you see. Let me heat a pizza on the ground. When I get this that low, man, you would heat a pizza. You put a pizza like a poison on a piece of sandpaper.
Did they play a lot of clarinet in the low register?

No. I don't remember anybody playing clarinet in the low register until I started playing. I never, none of nobody else in the register and above the register. In fact, I'll tell you about myself, I'm not much above the register. It's good enough with a full orchestra, you know, the bigger band. But whether you take, for instance, you take a short band, it's disagreeable. You understand? Not to get way up, man. You can go maybe a portion of it, but you shouldn't go up as you, as you ought to, with a small band. Because there's nothing between that, you understand? In other words, it's like, for instance, I call it myself, like a man going up a ladder. See, if you're going up a ladder, you got a step to go, going up a step. If you miss one step, there's a little way up there, well, that's missing. That's what you're opening. You should go up there, if you're going to miss that, you might fall. You understand? So all you do is take it easy. Now, if you got a good, you want to read a good bunch of men's day, well, you go what you want. You know? See, when you're all, in other words, you're organized. When you're organized, you can turn your back. The band be here, you'll be across the street. You'll know the time is starting, the time is off. You wouldn't need anybody to tell you that. You know, your feelings will tell it, if you got it in you. Now, you take a long time, there's some men to read music, you take the music man and they turn around on him, you give them all the trouble in the world. You know, he's looking at their music, their music's gone, he's gone. You know, it's the same, identical. That's where I feel about it. I don't have other stages, but I feel about it because I've been through it. I've been through it. You can take another man and say, this is my house. I'll come in here and put a little light on, walk in here, I ain't gonna stumble over nothing. You gonna come in here and stumble. That's where I feel about it. I don't think you can get around it. You take a bunch now, alright, when I was with you, with Kelley's band. That was a bunch of men that actually knew each other. They actually knew each other, you didn't have a worry. I see we used to pull jobs off. If man or two, three, one or two men's is missing, he's behind time. We didn't pay no more. He cared a job more. When he got these, you know, man, I'm sure glad you all started. Late Sunday, everything's alright. Everybody's pleased. Someone would criticize, oh, we didn't miss you. All like that. Don't get there when he said, we miss him, we working. After he got there, well, he find a different house. Take a bunch of men, the best thing in the world for any man that's playing music to have a regular band. Sturdy man. There's no sense in you, cause he's good. You can take the best man and put him with the worst, son. He ain't no good. He ain't no good without it just got it in him. If he got it in him, he'll hang on for a while, then he'll come in. But outside of that, he's gonna have some trouble. He's gonna get to say, oh, you ain't doing this right. You oughta do it like this. You oughta do it like that. He's gonna have some complaint. See that often, man. I betcha if I had this, I'd do this. I betcha if I had this, I'd do this. I betcha if I had this, I'd betcha if I had this. I betcha if I had this. I betcha if I had this. I betcha if I had this. I betcha if I had this. I betcha if I had that. That's all that. You know, just a long time ago, we get on the advertising, alright? Pull five bands out, every band's out, dip in harm. But we fight, we fightin' for that date. Who can get the best crown in there? We don't look for the weaker band we can win. We want to find the weaker band and all that shit. We want the strong band. Get up and get the strongest band you can get. Right on up there, battle them on out, let the crowd see for they sell. You take people out of here, band of here, man, and say, he's the only band, that's the best band of all. Something like that. You take a bunch of them and put them together.
You know, I was wondering, how soft would they entertain in those old days? Would they always play the last chorus real loud or would they play it soft or what?
No, the last chorus is loud.
They would play it loud now?
It's loud heavy, yeah. Always going heavy.
Always going heavy.

Always going heavy. You see, President, you see, just about the, in the chorus of a tune, just about the middle of a tune, you fall soft. You understand, just about halfway, you get on soft with it. Now when you get near to the last of you, come on up, get on up to your right man and knock off, go out heavy. And that's the way it went. And that was with most all of the bands, most of the every band they had. And I know I played with most of every band in the city and out of the city. I played with everything. This wasn't much on parades. The parades that I did play in meant it's buddied. You know that I liked it or wanted to be with, when I was awake with the others, man, I couldn't make it. I always thought it was too hard. It's just a subtle beat. You read out and get it hot and it'll blister you. When it's blistered, you got it. Your carpet top didn't mean any good because it got hot too. I was just taking our crown and holding it on the mud piece and put it on the arm and walk with it. Something hit me.
Who did you play parades with?
I played parades with most everything I had here. Most everything I had here.
Did you play with the Excelsior?
I played most everything I had here. I went to every band that you mentioned, Innocent and all the others that say.
What, did you play E flat ever?

I never used an E flat. I used a B flat. It was a... E flat, I had an E flat and I gave it away. I don't know if they many men use E flat now. Most of them are playing with B flat. Of course, when I was playing in Scotch music I used a B. I had A and B and then time we used A and B. I used a B and then time we used a B. I used a B. I used a B. I take and pull out all my... No, sorry. I just take and pull out just about... About that much you say. About that much you say on each joint. And I'll get my right tune up. Or I have to watch it. I'm doing G, D, A, C anyway. You pull out about a... About that much you say on each joint. And I'll get my right tune up. Or I have to watch it. I'm doing G, D, A, C anyway. You pull out about a quarter of an inch or something? Just about that much on each joint. I can't see it man. About a half inch or quarter of an inch? No, no. This is not quite a quarter you can see. Oh yeah, I see. About a fourth. Mm-hmm.
You pull out that much on each joint and you're going to pitch any key, you can pitch the key they got.
And the only trouble is to hold it.
Now you catch any key they playing. I don't know about now.
Because I don't know how the instruments run now. They made so much different. But then time they used A and B.
Otherwise a C.

That covered everything. And you can't see it. That's not much on each joint. That much on each joint. I can't see it man. About a half inch or quarter of an inch? No, no. It's not quite a quarter you can see. Oh yeah, I see. About a fourth. But that much on each joint and you're going to pitch any key, you can pitch the key they got. And the only trouble is to hold it. Now you catch any key they playing. I don't know about now. Because I don't know how the instruments run now. But you had a C. She covered everything. Now E flat. Well some of them would use E flat in praise. You know like the professors. They call it an E flat. Like we call it something. We didn't want an E flat. We took a B flat.
Who were some of the other clarinet players in town in the 20s?

Well I don't know. In the 20s I believe we had Art and Hale. Here we had Jimbo. Yeah Jimbo was out here in the 20s. Now here we had Johnny Hunnicall. Johnny Dots. Johnny Dots. We had Pills. And uh. Had this other boy Zeb. Had Zeb. Then this boy Joe Watson. Had him. And uh. Kaiser. We had Kaiser. We had Georgie boy.
What kind of a clarinet player was Georgie Boyd? John Boyd was a pretty good clarinet player. Would you say he had a rough style?

Well yeah his style was more rough than I was. Rougher than you? Yeah. He's a hard clarinet player. Was he strong? He's pretty strong. But I got to lean on all of them. I didn't ask for it or say I had it. They gave it to me. On Hale I didn't know. After I was playing a whole lot of clarinet. And that time. They had a good little clarinet play some of them boys. I can't remember. Who were the ones that you liked especially? In clarinet? Well the one I liked in clarinet really was uh. I say for instance you say like. In clarinet playing. Well I liked it George Brackey. I was crazy for George Brackey. I thought he was one of him and the big idol. Louie not to know what I mean dear
Walter Barnes was away? Where was he from? He was from St. Charles or Lake Charles. He got killed in a fire.
In Natchez. He was a clarinet player? Was he a good one? Good clarinet player.
Did he play around New Orleans much? All those fellas, they didn't see him. They come on down here. We went on up there.
Did the Walter Barnes live here or did he just come in on gigs? No, no. He stayed up there in Natchez.
How about Bacay? What were some of the things you liked about the way Bacay played? Peter Bacay? No, George Bacay. What? Bacay. Bacay. Oh, George? Yeah.

Well, I'll tell you how George was. He was a, to me he was a sweet clarinet player. You know, he just took his time and made that. You know, he didn't rough it out. But he had that one way. Now for a band man, he wasn't that much, he ain't a band man. But he was a tough man in the parade. And you could hear him way down there but so sweet. Now your man, your good band man, real band man, that was Louis, which we called Big Eye Louis. In the orchestra you mean? Yeah. In the orchestra. That's really, Charlie can tell you that. He's a real band man. You like this style, huh? What kind of a style did he have then? Yeah, the swing style, the sweet style. It's like I play, I don't play one way. I play different. I wish I could. I'll have to shorten up a little bit. I'll try to shorten up to get some of my stuff. Yeah. Different way of playing, you know. Not one style play. I never liked one style play.

You know that time you cut the records with Charlie Love? Do you remember that? Was it on St. Louis Street near Decatur? That's right, yeah. Uh huh. Well it seemed to me as the evening went on, you changed your whole tone and style and everything, you know? Yeah. You played different. I could just imagine, I could just sit down here and just imagine, I could see all through Merlin Boys and over the Rhine, Spanish food man, West End, all in places. Boy, no.

Stag. It wasn't stag dance. Winners, winners, and maybe a little gravy and macaroni, or have somebody to cook the dinner, have somebody to cook for them. See that place, Lucian Tenor, out here on Dolphin and Legion Field? We met, we were playing there for years. Right across in the square.
I know that home.
You know it?
Portuguese.
That's what they call it?

Quiet fellas, huh?

Thanks.

Oh yeah, I know that school.

They had us, but dances in the school? That's right.

That's right, and that would be twice a month. Oh yeah, that wrist ring up our bones, don't forget. That's when I'm going to be there. I know that, but we couldn't buy that date for nothing. This boy died, Plessy, how they call him, Joe Plessy? I believe he died, he used to play trombone. Yeah, I heard of him. He used to be at our dance all the time. He's supposed to be a nice guy.
Joe?

Oh man, that's a fine boy. That's fine, trombone. I seen Joe died, you heard that? I believe so. I think I heard it, but I heard that afterwards. I knew them boys, I knew, man, that, uh, I knew if they got away from me, mind me being scattered, but they used to, they'd go, they'd come up, we'd be talking, they'd come up to me. Used to, uh, had the Lucian tenor, we used to play there, then we used to play up in the Irish Channel. Yards up in there, man, at lawn parties. Started playing at eight o'clock, and ended up about six in the morning. You couldn't go when they got you there, but they paid you all right. They treated you all right. Got anything you wanted, more than what you could handle. More than you could handle, and you were treated for each class. But you couldn't go, you had to stay there and play. But I didn't mean, uh, just keep playing, you know, play on this like your regular time of playing. White and black was the same thing, because you gave up all the here. You played for white, when you look up, there's much black as they had white. You played over there for white, and you got there as much black as they had white. All they want is don't you touch it either. Don't interfere with it. You know, the Irish Channel used to be tough up there. No policeman didn't go up there. You go up there, you had to go up there like a gentleman with his hat in his hand. There'd be a fight between them. You two fight, go ahead and fight. You have to fight. No knife, no gun or nothing. This state ain't fight. See when he got whipsy, oh that's all I gotta know. Shake hands. Let's go to this. Now they don't want to hear that no more. Don't want to hear it no more. They'll come up there, you my buddy, beat my friend up and all that. Uh-uh. You want to fight? Play and fight. That's the way it was. I remember one time we played at the lake. I'll never forget this as long as I've been. Uh, this boy, Edward Gasper was playing drums and that boy used to keep a beautiful set of drums. I knew him, dumb man, was a, oh, really beautiful. So, uh, somehow or another, we were playing that food at the Donate at the, uh, Spanish Food. Well, our camp went down the run and our camp set off this run. Another run, the run down there, the other camp come in this. That they make the boot of the band fight each other right from the back. You know man, we played over, I don't know if it was shocking them or who it was, I can't just remember. But when we got there, we had a habit, we test the band out. See, we tune with the band out, we had a band over there, man, we bust loose and running about three or four hard numbers. Man, they get hot, they start to bust now. Well, we know how strong it was when they played. It was blow down on them. Man, they get hot, man, they be playing and blowing at us, man. We wouldn't pay them to mind. Now, when they slept, we'd shake them up a little bit. Part of that evening, come on, they all would come up. Their band was better than our band. They left them way around then, come to our camp and save that. Part of when they come there with that, they start all home, they start the free for all. Now, this was the run coming right in here. And all the hall was in the center like this, you know. This was the hall here, the house, and all around here was the gallery. This was the run going through. Man, they started fighting, free for all. All around there, man, I had twice drumming, man. I couldn't get out with it, no way. When I did get out with it, took a run on the run. Man, they fit there, the policeman come there, man. They threw him in the lake. Then the crowd come there, man. I'll never forget the one in there. When we did get away, they settled out. They put a couple of them in jail, man. So the woman we was playing for, she'd come back. She had to run down.
She said, you all got everything? You got all this stuff? Yeah, we got everything.

Oh, why that dirty thing? What did they come over here and let her lost for? Well, I just broke it up. She paid us off. One of the women's got a beautiful wristwatch. She lost that wristwatch and a fellow picked it up. So he said, if anybody ever asked for it, they tell him, oh God. I'm glad, I believe I know who it is. That was a free fall. All around the camp and couldn't get up. Beating up each other, throwing each other in the lake and all that. The whole gallery was filled with people? Jam. Jam, man. A free fall. You know how it did? That old crowd come over here to jump on this crowd and the boat had a good crowd. Showed the police and when he come back. He had to come back to jail. How did they take him to jail? How did they take him to jail? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
in those times. Patrol way. They didn't put them on the train then? No, no, it was out the west end.

When I got to my drum and get to working with my drums and my piano, I knew they was going to work there. They'd pull them. They'd be like, you know, I'd always get to work there. I'd always get to work there. I'd always get to work there. I'd always get to work there. What drummers did you like to work with? Well I had pretty good drummers, most every drum I worked with. Yeah, I had pretty good drummers, most every drum I worked with. I worked with Happy, Benny, Red Happy, a little happy to be up here, which is the Red Happy anyway. And this Happy used to be up here, with Bill. Which Happy?
That's Black Happy?
Black Happy. And I worked with Benny, Dave Bailey, Cy Frazier, and Faith So. I don't know, I worked with the Grocey, everything they had here. Every drummer had a record. I worked with them.
Who did Dave Bailey play with?
Dave played with many bands, many, many bands. You might say he plays with I believe the Rinker Band now. Gibson.
Gibson? Yeah, a non-union band. Non-union?
That's who he played with? Well he's a good drummer. He was a good drummer, I can tell you that.
He was lively and still, you know.

Well on the stand, on the music stand, he stood lively. He stayed there and he danced on them drums and he had everything going and his temper was there and he never nausea out. Never get up on that cymbal and swing your eye on him, man. He worked that cymbal in there, he stood there dancing on him, he exploded like a fool and bust out and laughed. He said, he said, how about you, brother-in-law, let's go. He's gone now. Last time my son, I said no, he said he ain't playing nothing, just one or two tunes, he ain't been playing with no bands or nothing. He said you like to work with the banjo. Who are some of the different banjo players that you played with? Well I worked with many, many banjos. Little Dad and well my cousin, you know that. And uh... Which cousin? Lawrence. Wake with Lawrence and wake with John too. Lawrence is way behind, Lawrence is wake with John in my class.
I don't know, but many of them wake with...

A whole lot of those fellas I don't forget, Gusu and... Got some, huh? A whole gang of most everything, everything in that time, in that class. They're not a man of no kind. Piano players, no. Little Mikey died, two Mikey died. Wake with them. Bob ran, the weak head Bob ran out. Who is that?
Which one? T-Boy.
T-Boy we called, what, Paul? Yeah. I said T-Boy, it's an old little kid name and stuff.
Yeah.
But Bob ran out, Paul Bob ran out, but we didn't say that. We said T-Boy Bob ran.
He was young then, huh? Mm-hmm.
Called him T-Boy and called his sister T-Gal. And the old man was always old man Bob ran. Even when he was young.
Mm-hmm.

That's right. He's got a little kid, Shani. Drink that on wine, man. I don't know how those fellas do it. They just leave themselves go like that. One. I believe I almost started drinking wine. I believe I started drinking wine. I didn't know you drank wine ever. I didn't know you drank wine ever. I don't know. I don't know how those fellas do it. They just leave themselves go like that. Wine. I believe I almost started drinking wine. I didn't know you drank wine.
Around the apex? Remember that night? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. I remember that night. Harrison's daughter was there that night. Yeah, I remember that night.
Harrison's daughter was there that night. Uh-huh. Yeah, I remember that night. Yeah, I forgot all about that. I started drinking wine. Yeah? I believe I started drinking wine.
I didn't know you drank wine ever. I did see you drank a little blood around Apex.
Around Apex?
Remember that night?
Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, I remember that night.
Harrison's daughter was there that night.

Uh-huh. Yeah, I forgot all about that. I asked one thing about it. Most anybody you meet know me. All the musicians know me. Don't talk about the public, because they really know me. I mean, from the older one down to the young one, a whole lot of them got confidence. They think I can play yet, or some of them believe I'm playing yet. They played at the Palace Show, Palace Seattle, I don't know. When I played down there, they kept the spotlight on me. Kept it on me. Forced me for solos, and all the girls were crazy about me. The manager was crazy about me. Howard, man, let me tell you, that's all they say.
What band was that?
Well, Howard had that in charge, Kid Thomas. This was a big man to wait for the show.
Kid Howard had it? Yeah.

We put up a long time in the show there. Was it a good band? Yeah, we had a good band in there. That little kid he called Joe on drums. And, uh, let me see who it was. Had Joe, they had Howard. Had Howard.
Drew Howard, Paul. Myself. What was Paul playing?
I had to call him on piano. Oh, how do you call that? Paul. I can't call his name, no. He was on piano, and Willie Foster was on drums. He was on the violin.
We had a good band in there.

Was that your brother, Paul? Mm-hmm. He was on sax. Did you play a lot of jazz? Oh, man, when that jazz would come on there, they'd turn the show up. When that would start, I'd get it. I'd scream and dance, I'd stop them all day. That was before the show, you'd start up there, swing a couple of numbers, and come down to
the show. You were playing solos in those days, huh? Yeah, we played plenty. Well, with bands like Buddy Petit's band, did you take any solos?

Well, them solos weren't much in that time. We didn't take solos. You know, on the solos it took itself, it was on the music, the coffers, you know. But this solo was by yourself. It didn't do that. This man would get tired of so many bars, he would play, he'd get tired, well, to keep his lip from swelling or something, well, he'd pull down, take a chance, but the time he'd come up, you'd felt that way, you'd take down, take a chance. And then, you know, the solo, and then, well, it was on the music. But all that solo part, that stuff come out, that's where other men get ideas on you, to know what you're doing. That's all that was for.
I know on the records you made, you took a lot of solos.

Well, they asked for solos on them records, too, on them records, a certain part of it. But I never believed in solos that way. But how we used to do it a long time ago, when they'd turn it over to me, the point of thing you say, like me, and the drums would get on low and pedal, and they'll get to our bass and piano. See, when we had that, you understand? Well, that was the only solo that we would have to take. Well, after we had a special number we'd play, take and let the banjo or guitar or piano do so much on it, and we'd give them a break in it and do so much, give them a break and do so much and take off. Yeah, there's many, many, many musicians, man. I can't call the name of it. All of the Bob Pickett and all that old bunch up there, man. That's all old time musicians. K-2, man. K-2, oh man, I can't call the name of it. What did Bob Pickett call it? Bob was a bass. I was a bass. He played the bass player. He played the bass player. I never heard of him. He played the bass player. Who did he work with? Well, a different band. He played the bass player. He played the bass player. I never heard of him. He played the bass player. Who did he work with? Well, a different band. See, that was a whole lot around there. They had a band up there too. See, it was a, in them time it was, it was a big, it was a big, it was a big, it was a tough one. like the bands on the other side of Clown Street, where you see that band, we'd be friends and all, but you know, like a distant friend. They didn't want much with the bands on this side. You know what I mean? Well out there had a couple of men in there they liked, right there, to really use them. But they were never frightened or nothing like that, but you know, just a distant friend.
But you were on the downtown side of Canal Street, right?

I stood. I stood, but I was all over. I was over the river, I was trying to cut off a down low coast, I was up the coast. Up around General Arnold, Loke, Chula Irish General, man, on the back of Padres, and the cab rest in the tongue. Got it all off, am I, boy?
I don't know what I got in my head. I don't know what I got in my head. Mm-hmm. Pretty good, man. That's where the down.
Good evening, man.
Howdy, how you been, Bonds?
I had a shot in my drink, I don't let a cough. Huh?
Just let me know. What'd you say?
What'd you say?
Yeah, let's find out something about those mutes. When you didn't have a derby, what would you do?

Well, if you didn't have a derby, we could use anything you could get your hand on, like a bucket or a can or something like that, you know? Or even if they had a luminal derby there, we'd use that. Sometimes it's feeling good, except I don't know. Hello? Aubrey, go outside.
Alright.

We'd, uh, just step over like he'd got his mute thing, and walk on over to it and use it a few seconds. Sometimes we'd double up, the reglas would double up, you know, put them all together. Get a kick out of that.
What kind of a tone would you get with a mute?
Every tone.
Would it sound anything like a sax?
Probably, it'd go deeper than the sax. A little deeper, you know?
I wanted to ask you, let's see, you said you were born on Claiborne Street?
Claiborne Avenue? I was born in, uh, in Climbit.
And did you grow up in that house?
No, I probably just grew up to, uh, to Lauderd Street, about seven, eight years old.
What was your father's name? Did he, he lived there in that house?
Same, it's the same as my name.
Emil Vox.
That's right. But all the trouble, he was like Paul, he got Daniel.
Emil Daniel? Mm-hmm.
That's where Paul is, Paul Daniel. You see?
So you each got a piece of his name. And, uh, after you moved from there, where did you move to?
Well, when we moved from there, we moved to the Poot Street. And Poot and what?
Poot and what?
Poot between the building and, uh, Robert.
And how old were you, uh, while you were living there?
Well, I lived in there? Well, I don't know, I think I stood there maybe about two or three years.
Was that short pants or long pants?
No, that was short pants.
And then after you moved, uh, from Port, where did you move?

When I moved from Poot Street, let's see. I moved, I come up to El Monster Avenue. Yeah, El Monster Avenue. I moved the same number. No, yeah. 14, 16, Poot Street, 14, 16, El Monster Avenue. I'll never forget that.
And how old were you when you were living on El Monster Avenue?
Oh, I don't know, I think I was about 16.
Were you playing music then?
I was playing on music, I was blowing.
You were blowing, huh?
Yeah, playing on the band.
Were you working with bands at all? Were you blowing with bands?
No, I wasn't blowing with no bands. Sometimes they'd take me out, I wouldn't call out of there.
But you weren't getting paid, right? No.

I didn't get paid when I went to the district playing. I was picked up and I was playing, and they needed to sit in the district. All we done took a fair long pass and made them, made them a pittance by cutting them down, put them on, went on up there and played, but we didn't get paid. But it was alright enough for us to stay on the job until they get back. And after the time for them to knock off, when they got back.
Who was some of the other men in the bands when you went to play in the district? Some of them bands?

Well, when I went up there, Joe Oliver, Joe Oliver, let's see. You gotta remember now. I know T.O. was out there. T.O., Louie. T.O., Louie and Rocky. Them, them were the places we would go. Do they have little short bands or big orchestras? Well, they run into five piece bands. Back to Almas Avenue, how old were you when you moved away from there? Mm-hm, I didn't sit around there. I don't remember that. It was good.
Where did you move to after that?
I was coming to Burry, between Spain and Simran.
And you stood there a while?
I stood there quite a while. And after time I started playing.

That's when you started really playing. Really playing. And where did you move from there? See, we got to the city directly. We can tell the exact date, you know, where you lived. You know, by looking your name up.
Yeah. The part that got me on back. Yeah, you got me there on Spain and Burry.
We'll have to look it all up and then come down and show you. And you can figure out when you lived in different places, who you were playing with. How long did you live on the harbor?
Let's see, I moved from the middle of the block to the corner.
On Burry, huh?
Burry in Spain.
And who were you playing with when you lived on Burry?
I played with most anybody.
Everybody, huh?
Yeah, mostly everything was. I was fitting.
Well, let's go back to the district. Wow. How much of the work was in the district? Would you say many musicians were there? Not too many?
Good many.
How many? Good many.
Yeah, good many musicians. Most every house had it. Had music up there. Every house, you know every place. Gammon houses.
You said there were about a dozen bands there, or two dozen?
Oh, about two dozen.
About two dozen bands.

Around the neighborhood. All through where Crosswood, where the Thomas Station is now. Over on Ramport Street. Go down to what you call St. Claude Street there. Basin Street there. What the name you call it. Way back to Robson Street. Come back to Corney, St. Louis. And you go all the way back and you hit on the other side there. You had the Red District. I played all through there. I played all through there. All in the tunks. The cabras in the tunks too, in the barms.
Well, would they have a every night a week job, or would it be three nights a week, or what?
Every night a week.
They'd be jumping every night in the house.
And you say they used mostly five pieces? Mostly five pieces, yeah.
No, some.
Give me that. What would they have in the band?

What instruments? Well, I would have the cabra piano, and carolets, trumpets, trombone. Some would have this bass guitar and violin. Some would just have maybe this piano drumming, clarolets. Or maybe trumpet. You know what I'm saying? Three piece. Some would have this piano.
You think there'd be a hundred musicians working in now? You think there'd be fifty, or what number one?
Oh, there'd be a hundred conks. The little ones in the papers.
Conks, the piano players and everything.
Yeah.

Well, how many musicians you figure there were in New Orleans at that time? That would be a question. That would be part of the work, but it wouldn't be nearly all of it. You had a hundred guys probably playing in brass bands, too, huh?

Well, the brass band wasn't a brass band was equalized to the string band. That band was splitting. See, if a man played a funeral or prayed or something like that, well, that day, he'd come to that job that night. See, so you couldn't count that. There's two.
Oh, yeah.
One, yeah.

I see. But that's not what I mean. I'm trying to figure out where most of your work would be in those days. See, the average musician, would he be working mostly in the street or mostly picnics or mostly...
Mostly cabarets. Mostly cabarets.
Mostly cabarets.
Yeah. Mostly cabarets. And where would those cabarets be?
In the district? All through that district. Some different spots in town.

Maybe magazines, street, or the pole in the avenue. Some places up there would have spots with music in it. All up on General Arnold, spots up there with music in it. Take back on Perdita Street and all them streets, Franklin, Grave, you know. See what you mean? Yeah, all of them had it all over Ramport Street. Dryads. Most of them places had the same thing. Three or four piece band, maybe just a piano and drum. Maybe just a five piece band. What about the Red Onion? What would they have in that? Well, you probably got that. I don't think I can give you anything on that. You never went to Red Onion? You never went to Red Onion? No, where's that at?
It was on Ramport, I think about 800-700- lies.

Well, I'mma be right with it for the caller no getting on their name to sing that I got away from me. Yeah, that's away from me. I couldn't come up to it. Not with the truth. See, I couldn't come up to it with the truth. I know most of the places I know.
Spanos, you don't remember?
I don't know Spanos. What was that? Well, that is the same thing. That's a tunk. What do they have? What we call it, tunk and cabaret. Cabaret is a higher grade than what the tunk was.
Would they have a full band and Spanos or piano or what?
Yeah, about a three-piece band. Take maybe a trumpet, you know. Piano and drum. Most of them was piano, drum, clarinet, trumpet, something like that.
Do they have any really ratty brass bands here? You know, that really played tunk music in the streets?
Well, yeah. All the same men that played jazz bands played the same music.
I'm talking about, say, in 1910 when you were just really coming out, who would be in the street playing really tunk music?
Well, we had a good men up in there. You had Joe Oliver Day, you had Manuel Perez, you had Kimmer, you had Icon White. Oh, I couldn't get you the names of all of them.
Yeah, but I mean, non-reading bands, ones that didn't read at all, wouldn't they have those?
Well, that's a pretty tough one. Most of them had something.
They had some guys that were doing.

They all had something. They wasn't professional. You see, you take a man in them time, if he was in, uh, 7th or 6th grade age, he wouldn't say anything about musicians. You understand? It's like a man, a priest or a preacher or something. You know that, you know, when you put yourself there, you put yourself up against something. I call it the same thing. You catch a man up in there, well, he, he take a piece of music and he sit down and he figure it out and he go on, he go on it and then he take it and he run it over it. Well, he fight that fight until he get it. When he get it, it might be something in there hard for him to memorize. See, well, when he get to playing it, then, what you gonna play? Oh, 27. He said, man, this darn thing is with me so much, man, I'm scared of it. He run over, he correct that part then and say, let's go. Well, that's actually correct, but if you take a man that's reading music, what you got, 27? You all ready? All right.
Did Chris have a brass band, Chris Kelly? No. He would never play a little jump up job or anything like that, huh?
No, he always hired him on that. Did he read? Yeah, spell.
What about Buddy? Did he get out in the street much? Buddy?

Oh, he was a parade man. Buddy was more parade man than what Kelly was. Kelly was a parade man too, but he wasn't like Buddy. The man, huh, Joe Olive. They say Walter Bloom, wasn't it? That man was invited parade, you see? He was a good man and more, I was calling the name, but I can't think of.
I think we better call it to a halt, that's about the end of this reel. I think four reels will be enough for a day. We sure do appreciate it.
Well, that's the best I could do, to think of that neighbor. Oh, well, it was fun. To get all that together, you might get something out of it.
We'll get some more later.

segments.title: Opening: address, date and name for the recording
segments.summary: Dick Allen sets up the recording at Barnes's house, notes the date and has him give his name and its spelling; Herb Freewell introduces himself.

segments.title: Birthplace and birth date
segments.summary: Barnes says he was born at Cluett and Claiborne on 18 February 1892, making him 68.

segments.title: Uncle Taton Bonds and his string band
segments.summary: His uncle played with bass, guitar, mandolin and violin, mostly by ear, with no trumpets, at parties and serenades; Barnes was a small child when he died.

segments.title: Valve trombone and Long Charlie
segments.summary: Barnes recalls the valve trombone, fingered like a trumpet with no slide, played by Long Charlie and used more like a bass part.

segments.title: Valve players and Ambrose Powers
segments.summary: Discussion of valve players like Cornish and Deucon; Ambrose Powers, uncle of Toka, played guitar, violin, trombone and mandolin and first took Barnes out.

segments.title: Playing with Ambrose's band
segments.summary: Barnes recalls his first work with Ambrose, who played violin, and the guitar and bass players in that band.

segments.title: The Golden Rule, Imperial, Superior and Boys in Blue bands
segments.summary: Barnes names bands of the period and their leaders: Buddy Petit's Boys in Blue, Sugar Johnny's Imperial, and the Golden Rule with swapping personnel.

segments.title: Tunes played and bands competing on Sundays
segments.summary: He cannot recall the tune names, mentions Scott Joplin music, and describes bands showing off for club crowds on Sundays.

segments.title: Clarinet trios without drums or horns
segments.summary: Small groups of two or three clarinets or a bass played with no drums, trombones or cornets, and no swing.

segments.title: Soft music, blues and introductions
segments.summary: Barnes says his uncle's band played soft music for surprise parties, and explains blues played with an introduction.

segments.title: Dynamics: soft in the middle, loud on the last chorus
segments.summary: He explains how bands played loud, dropped soft mid-tune and went out heavy, and that nobody played clarinet in the low register before him.

segments.title: Parades and pitching a B flat clarinet
segments.summary: He played parades with most bands, never used E flat, and describes adjusting joints of a B flat clarinet to pitch any key.

segments.title: Clarinetists of the 1920s and Georgie Boyd
segments.summary: Barnes lists clarinet players in town in the 1920s including Jimbo, Johnny Dots, Pills, Zeb and Joe Watson, and calls George Boyd rougher than himself.

segments.title: Walter Barnes and George Baquet
segments.summary: Walter Barnes of Natchez was a good clarinetist who died in a fire; George Baquet was a sweet player and parade man, while Big Eye Louis was the real band man.

segments.title: Low-register playing with a derby mute
segments.summary: Allen recalls the Charlie Love record session; Barnes explains his low-register clarinet played into a felt derby, which no one else did until his records.

segments.title: Strong clarinetists: Pills, Jimbo and George Lewis
segments.summary: He liked Pills, found Jimbo timid, does not remember George Lewis from then, and notes the men who left town.

segments.title: Nicknames and meeting at headquarters
segments.summary: Nobody knew musicians' real names; players were found at corner headquarters, and the jobs included picnics, balls and weddings.

segments.title: Street noise and a fish vendor
segments.summary: Chatter about a fish seller with a loudspeaker truck, haggling over price, breaking the interview.

segments.title: Dances and food at the clubs
segments.summary: Barnes describes who danced and the food and drink served at the dances where the bands played.

segments.title: Dances at the school with Buddy Petit
segments.summary: He recalls playing for years at neighbourhood dances including a school hall, with Buddy Petit, and remembers trombonist Joe Plessy.

segments.title: A rowdy dance, the jail and Buddy Petit's band
segments.summary: Story of a dance that ended in a fight and lost watch, arrests held at a west end jail, and Buddy Petit leading the band.

segments.title: Kid Thomas and his clarinetists
segments.summary: Barnes played with Kid Thomas early on; they list clarinetists in Thomas's band, including Paul Barnes.

segments.title: Dislike of saxophone and modern amplified music
segments.summary: Barnes says the saxophone makes players lazy, complains about modern playing and electric instruments, and that everyone thinks they can sing.

segments.title: Singers and concerts in the old days
segments.summary: Barnes says bands were hired to play, not sing, and then rambles about a music box he broke.

segments.title: Guitar and banjo; electric guitar
segments.summary: He says electric guitars came in about 10 or 12 years ago, preceded by guitar, banjo, then guitar; he preferred the banjo.

segments.title: Saxophone can be played well
segments.summary: Short exchange where Barnes agrees a saxophone can be played well.

segments.title: Lessons from Picou, Bechet and Ory; Jimbo; California
segments.summary: Barnes took lessons from Picou with Sidney Bechet, discusses who left New Orleans and prospered, Ory and Jimbo, and his visit to California.

segments.title: Gut-bucket clarinet and the drummers he worked with
segments.summary: Barnes says he drove bands to play, names drummers such as Black Happy and Dave Bailey, and praises Dave's lively drumming.

segments.title: The Barbarins: T-Boy and T-Gal
segments.summary: He recalls piano players and the Barbarin family, T-Boy (Paul), his sister T-Gal and old man Barbarin.

segments.title: Drinking wine and his reputation
segments.summary: The talk turns to musicians drinking wine and a night at Apex; Barnes says all musicians know him and some think he still plays.

segments.title: Kid Howard's band at the show
segments.summary: Barnes recalls a show band led by Kid Howard in which he soloed, with his brother Paul on sax and Willie Foster on drums.

segments.title: Taking solos in Buddy Petit's day and on records
segments.summary: He says solos were rare in early bands, only breaks for banjo, piano and others, and he did not believe in them.

segments.title: Downtown New Orleans and a visitor
segments.summary: Brief remarks about working all over town and a visitor greeting during the recording.

segments.title: Using a derby or bucket as a mute
segments.summary: Without a derby, players used buckets or cans as mutes; the tone was deeper than a sax.

segments.title: Childhood homes and his father's name
segments.summary: Barnes lists where he grew up, starting on Claiborne and moving to Lauderd and Poot Streets, and says his father shared his name.

segments.title: Moving address by address and starting to play
segments.summary: He moves to El Monster Avenue at about 16, plays without pay in the district, and then on Burry and Spain Street begins playing in earnest.

segments.title: How many bands worked the District
segments.summary: Barnes says about two dozen bands played in the Red District, in houses and honky-tonks.

segments.title: Every-night jobs and band sizes
segments.summary: Bands worked every night, usually five pieces, sometimes three, with piano, drums, clarinet, trumpet, trombone, guitar or violin.

segments.title: Counting musicians; cabarets and tunks
segments.summary: Allen asks how many musicians worked; Barnes says mostly cabarets and tunks, explains the difference and names the spots.

segments.title: Street bands and parade men
segments.summary: Barnes names street bandsmen and says Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly were parade men, Buddy more so.

segments.title: Closing of the reel
segments.summary: Allen ends the session at the end of the reel and thanks Barnes.
